project_name: Pinecrest Mill kraft lignin cake (fictional): dashboard assessment
disclaimers: Fictional demo data: the Pinecrest Mill and this lignin stream are invented. All values are illustrative assumptions, not measurements from any real mill, and must be replaced with a mill's own lab data before any decision.
BioValue AI gives indicative decision support. It does not guarantee profitability, does not verify customer demand, and does not constitute engineering approval.

Gross margin, profitability, NPV, and IRR are not calculated. They need capital costs, fixed costs, a discount rate, a time horizon, and agreed definitions, none of which are available yet. Gross contribution excludes capital costs, fixed costs, and the value of the feedstock in its current use.
Scores use a 1-5 scale. A criterion that was not assessed lowers data completeness; it is never counted as a low score.

constraints: Lignin leaves as wet cake, and no lignin dryer is available; buyers requiring dry powder would need to provide drying.
Solvent or membrane fractionation and chemical modification equipment are not available at the mill.
The recorded current route is internal boiler fuel, so diverting lignin to sale would change an existing fuel use.
Moisture is uncertain, affecting dry tonnage and shipped mass; verify it with mill measurements before planning logistics or product specifications.
Missing molecular-weight, phenolic-hydroxyl, and sodium measurements limit pathway and ash-related specification checks.
data_quality_notes: The record is fictional_demo, not measured; the mill and all profile values are invented illustrative assumptions and should not inform real decisions.
Molecular weight, phenolic hydroxyl content, and sodium are missing.
The lignin-content analytical method is stated only for illustration, and moisture is marked uncertain.
Validation passed the dry-matter balance, composition-total check, and data-gap coverage check; no failed checks or contradictions were reported.
agent.summary: Fictional demo profile: the recorded wet quantity and moisture convert to the values above, and the calculated dry mass agrees with the record. Validation found no inconsistencies, but the profile is not measured and has important composition and data-quality gaps.

data_gaps.impact: Every figure in this profile is invented for demonstration. Results based on it say nothing about a real mill.
data_gaps.next_step: Replace the profile with the mill's own lab data and production records.

data_gaps.impact: Molecular weight can't be compared with any pathway requirement until it is measured.
data_gaps.next_step: Commission a lab analysis of molecular weight distribution, and record the method used.

data_gaps.impact: Phenolic hydroxyl content can't be compared with any pathway requirement until it is measured.
data_gaps.next_step: Commission a lab analysis of hydroxyl group content, and record the method used.

data_gaps.impact: The make-up of the ash is unknown, so ash-related requirements can only be checked against total ash.
data_gaps.next_step: Request an inorganic element analysis of the ash.

data_gaps.impact: Reported lignin content depends on what the analysis counts. The method here is stated for illustration only.
data_gaps.next_step: Confirm the analytical method with the lab and use the same one when comparing with buyers' specifications.

data_gaps.impact: Moisture sets the dry tonnage (dry matter = wet quantity x (1 - moisture)) and the mass that has to be shipped.
data_gaps.next_step: Log cake moisture for each shift over at least one month.

checks.disclaimer: Fictional demo data: the Pinecrest Mill and this lignin stream are invented. All values are illustrative assumptions, not measurements from any real mill, and must be replaced with a mill's own lab data before any decision.

current_use.description: Fictional: the precipitated lignin is fired in the mill's own boilers in place of purchased fuel. The unit was built to relieve the recovery boiler, not to sell lignin.

geographic_market.logistics: Fictional: rail siding at the mill; the nearest deep-water port is assumed to be about 150 km away.

supported_claims.EV-PF-01#1: For kraft lignin in phenol-formaldehyde (PF) resins, the typical replacement of phenol is up to 50%, using a two-step process with depolymerized lignin (Mw 800-1,700 g/mol).
supported_claims.EV-PF-02#2: UPM states that LPF resin is industrially proven and meets EN 314-2 Bonding Class 3 for veneer plywood.
supported_claims.EV-PF-02#3: UPM reports formaldehyde emissions (EN 717-2) of 0.230 mg/m²/h for 12 mm spruce, 0.148 for 12 mm birch, and 0.170 for 12 mm combi panels made with LPF resin.
supported_claims.EV-PF-01#4: Global PF resin production was expected to reach about 10 Mt (valued at about USD 13.36 billion in 2019), and more than 50% of these resins are used to make adhesives for wood-based panels.
supported_claims.EV-PF-02#1: UPM states that its lignin can replace up to 80% of the phenol in lignin-phenol-formaldehyde (LPF) resin.
supported_claims.EV-PF-01#2: Kraft lignin needs an activation or depolymerization step before use in PF resins.
supported_claims.EV-PF-01#R1: Pre-treatment of kraft lignin: Activation or depolymerization is needed before kraft lignin is used in PF resins.
supported_claims.EV-PF-04#2: With the depolymerized lignin making up 50% of the phenolic component, the resin's viscosity, bonding strength, and free formaldehyde met the Chinese wood-adhesive standard used in the study.

applications.statement: Kraft lignin can be used as a partial phenol substitute in phenol-formaldehyde resin for plywood and other wood-panel adhesives.
The evidence also supports LPF resin for veneer plywood, including performance claims for bonding and formaldehyde emissions.

target_customers.statement: Plywood and other wood-based-panel producers are the implied customer types for lignin-based PF adhesives.

competing_materials.statement: The incumbent material being partly replaced is phenol in phenol-formaldehyde resin.

qualification_requirements.statement: Kraft lignin requires activation or depolymerization before PF resin use.
The cited plywood performance claims include EN 314-2 Bonding Class 3 and formaldehyde-emission testing under EN 717-2.
A laboratory study assessed resin properties against a Chinese wood-adhesive standard, but the paper names that standard inconsistently.

limitations: The reported high replacement levels, plywood performance, and cost savings include manufacturer claims; the vendor performance claims have no cited test report and concern UPM BioPiva, whose kraft status and composition are not specified.
The review's TRL rating applies to biobased phenolic resins generally, not specifically to kraft-lignin resin; its market-production forecast has no year attached, and its market value is from 2019.
The depolymerization study was laboratory-scale with poplar plywood samples, and the wood-adhesive standard is inconsistently identified.

The supplied feedstock profile says no mill dryer, fractionation, or chemical-modification equipment is available and identifies missing molecular-weight and phenolic-hydroxyl measurements; wet-cake moisture is uncertain.
missing_information: No named buyers, verified sales, buyer qualification pathway, current lignin or resin prices, contract terms, or regional demand estimates are provided.
The evidence does not establish whether this mill's wet cake meets a buyer's specifications or what drying and activation/depolymerization would cost.

market_evidence.rationale: Evidence includes an industrially proven LPF resin claim and established adhesive applications, but the record does not document lignin-resin sales by a producer or named buyers, so the evidence does not support the rubric's commercial-sales level.

supported_claims.EV-PU-01#1: Replacing 30 wt% of the petroleum-based polyol with unmodified lignin, 16 of the 19 lignins tested gave rigid PUR/PIR foams that passed all measured ASTM C1029-15 type 1 specifications.
supported_claims.EV-PU-02#1: Rigid foams containing 19-23% (w/w) hardwood kraft lignin, or 25-30% (w/w) organosolv lignin, kept comparable structure and strength.
supported_claims.EV-PU-03#1: Fifteen unmodified lignins (ten kraft, five organosolv) were tested as a replacement for 20 wt% of the petroleum-based polyol in flexible polyurethane foam.
supported_claims.EV-PU-03#3: Organosolv lignins were the most suitable for automotive flexible foam; kraft lignins gave denser, stiffer foams that the authors suggest may suit heavy-duty foams.
supported_claims.EV-PU-01#2: Two of the three foams that failed were made with kraft lignin; they failed the compressive strength and/or closed-cell content requirements.
supported_claims.EV-PU-04#R1: Modification of kraft lignin: Kraft lignin needs significant treatment (for example oxypropylation, depolymerization, or liquefaction) to reach target properties for polyurethanes.
supported_claims.EV-PU-03#2: Unmodified lignin reduced foam resiliency: compression set rose to 7-32% against 6% for the control, though it stayed within the standard's limit of below 60%.
supported_claims.EV-PU-05#1: Commercialization of lignin-based polyurethane foams remains limited by low product consistency, poor technical performance, and high production costs.
supported_claims.EV-PU-04#1: The IEA rates polyurethane uses of lignin (foams, panels, coatings, rubber replacement; kraft, organosolv, and soda lignin) at TRL 6.

applications.statement: Kraft lignin has been studied as a partial polyol replacement in rigid polyurethane/polyisocyanurate foams.
Unmodified lignin has also been studied in flexible polyurethane foam; the cited work suggests kraft lignin may suit denser, stiffer heavy-duty foams better than automotive flexible foam.

target_customers.statement: Rigid-foam producers, including producers serving insulation applications, are a potential customer type implied by the rigid PUR/PIR foam evidence.
Flexible-foam producers serving automotive or heavy-duty foam applications are potential customer types identified or implied by the cited study.

competing_materials.statement: The material being partly replaced is petroleum-based polyol.

qualification_requirements.statement: The rigid-foam study assessed ASTM C1029-15 type 1 specifications; some tested foams failed compressive-strength and/or closed-cell-content requirements.
The review says kraft lignin generally needs treatment such as oxypropylation, depolymerization, or liquefaction to reach polyurethane target properties.
The flexible-foam study compared compression set with a standard limit below 60%, but the cited evidence does not name the standard.

limitations: Much of the evidence is from laboratory foam studies; the rigid-foam results cover multiple lignin types and do not provide a kraft-only pass rate, while the 2013 rigid-foam study reports high-density foam and better performance for organosolv lignin.
The flexible-foam study compared laboratory foams with automotive OEM requirements; odor was not measured, and kraft lignin was associated with denser, stiffer foam and reduced resiliency.
The review's TRL applies to a broad set of polyurethane uses, not specifically to kraft-lignin foam; its replacement levels each come from a single cited study.
A review reports commercialization challenges including consistency, performance, and cost, but only its abstract was accessible.

The supplied feedstock profile says no mill dryer, fractionation, or chemical-modification equipment is available and identifies missing molecular-weight and phenolic-hydroxyl measurements; the stated missing phenolic-OH value does not establish total hydroxyl content.
missing_information: No named buyers, verified commercial sales, current lignin/polyol prices, contract terms, or regional demand estimates are provided.
The evidence does not establish performance or processing results for this mill's wet cake, or the costs of drying and the treatment needed for a specific polyurethane application.

market_evidence.rationale: The evidence shows research-scale testing and broad review discussion, but no documented lignin-foam pilots, development partnerships, or commercial sales; the review specifically describes commercialization as limited.

supported_claims.EV-CM-01#1: Oak Ridge National Laboratory (ORNL) specifications for lignin as a carbon fiber precursor (Baker et al. 2005) set lignin content at 99%, ash below 0.1%, volatiles below 5% at 250 °C, and full removal of particulates larger than 1 µm.
supported_claims.EV-CM-01#3: None of the lignin samples in the study met the ORNL volatiles specification.
supported_claims.EV-CM-02#4: Mechanical properties of lignin-based carbon fibers were about 50% of the target in this work.
supported_claims.EV-CM-04#2: Hard carbons from kraft lignin (carbonized at 1,200 °C) had higher initial coulombic efficiency than those from sulfonated lignin, which the review attributes to lower ash content.
supported_claims.EV-CM-06#2: Stora Enso announced a EUR 10 million pilot production line for lignin-based anode material, operational in 2021, with scale-up planned in standardized 20 kton manufacturing units.
supported_claims.EV-CM-05#1: Activated carbon has no strict limitations on precursor quality, so lignin too impure for other uses can be converted into it.
supported_claims.EV-CM-03#2: The modelled production cost of GreenLight lignin-based carbon fiber was EUR 12.6/kg, against about EUR 16/kg estimated for PAN-based fiber; cooperation with existing melt-spinning and carbon fiber plants could lower it to EUR 6.5-7.1/kg.
supported_claims.EV-CM-06#1: Stora Enso states that qualification with battery manufacturers and carmakers can take 3 years, and that partnering helps shorten this.
supported_claims.EV-CM-04#1: A feedstock comparison for sodium-ion battery hard carbon lists lignin at about 300 $/t with a carbon yield above 40%, against anthracite (50-200 $/t, about 90%) and cellulose (1,000 $/t, below 10%).
supported_claims.EV-CM-01#R1: Lignin content: Greater than 99% (ORNL precursor specification).
supported_claims.EV-CM-01#R2: Ash content: Below 0.1% by weight (ORNL precursor specification).
supported_claims.EV-CM-01#R3: Residual carbohydrates: Below 500 ppm (Baker 2011). Not mapped to the feedstock's carbohydrate percentage, because the source doesn't state the basis of the ppm figure.
supported_claims.EV-CM-01#R4: Volatile material: Below 5% at 250 °C. The feedstock profile has no volatiles field, so this is not checked.
supported_claims.EV-CM-01#R5: Particulate matter: 100% removal of particulates larger than 1 µm in diameter.
supported_claims.EV-CM-02#R1: Purification of kraft lignin: The kraft lignin examined needed purification before it could be used for carbon fiber.
supported_claims.EV-CM-02#R2: Melt spinnability of softwood lignin: A plasticizing (alloying) agent is needed to melt-spin softwood lignin.
supported_claims.EV-CM-05#R1: Precursor quality: No strict limitations on precursor quality; lower ash improves yield.
supported_claims.EV-CM-03#1: The GreenLight project raised the TRL of lignin precursor fiber production from 2-3 (proof of concept) to 5 (validated in an industrially relevant environment).

applications.statement: Lignin is supported as a precursor for carbon fiber, although the cited work documents substantial precursor and performance challenges.
Kraft lignin-derived hard carbon is discussed for sodium-ion batteries, and lignin-based anode material is also described for lithium-ion batteries.
Lignin can be converted to activated carbon, including when its precursor quality is unsuitable for more demanding uses.

target_customers.statement: Carbon-fiber producers and existing melt-spinning/carbon-fiber plants are potential customers or partners for lignin precursor fiber.
Battery manufacturers and carmakers are named as parties involved in qualifying lignin-based anode material.
Activated-carbon producers are an implied customer type for lignin-derived activated carbon.

competing_materials.statement: PAN-based fiber is a named comparison for carbon fiber.
Anthracite is listed as a competing hard-carbon feedstock for sodium-ion batteries.

qualification_requirements.statement: The cited ORNL carbon-fiber precursor specifications include lignin content greater than 99%, ash below 0.1% by weight, volatiles below 5% at 250 °C, removal of particulates larger than 1 µm, and residual carbohydrates below 500 ppm.
The examined kraft lignin required purification before carbon-fiber use; softwood lignin also required a plasticizing agent for melt spinning.

The records provide no equivalent formal precursor specification for hard carbon or activated carbon; the activated-carbon study reports no strict precursor-quality limits, while lower ash improves yield.
Battery-material qualification with manufacturers and carmakers is identified as a customer qualification step, but no technical standard is specified.

limitations: The carbon-fiber precursor specifications are cited secondhand and are not requirements for hard carbon or activated carbon; the carbon-fiber study used lignin from a non-standard kraft process, and none of its samples met the volatiles specification.
The DOE carbon-fiber progress-report findings are from 2009; its cost and mechanical-property figures are targets or results from that work, not current market evidence.
The GreenLight report is a project summary, its costs are modelled rather than measured, and its TRL applies to precursor fiber production rather than the full lignin-to-carbon-fiber chain.
The hard-carbon evidence is a review, and the activated-carbon evidence is a laboratory study using zinc chloride activation.
The battery pilot information is company investor material and describes plans as of 2021 whose later status was not verified; it provides no lignin quality specifications.

The supplied feedstock profile says no mill dryer or fractionation equipment is available, moisture is uncertain, and sodium measurements are missing; these issues are especially relevant to dry-mass logistics and ash-related specification checks.
missing_information: No verified current sales, named purchasing customers, contract terms, or regional demand estimates are provided; the battery pilot's later operating status is also unverified.

The evidence does not establish whether this mill's wet cake meets carbon-fiber purity specifications, what drying or purification would cost, or what battery and activated-carbon buyers would require for this feedstock.
Current prices and addressable volumes for lignin-derived hard carbon and activated carbon are not established by the evidence.

market_evidence.rationale: The evidence documents precursor-fiber development reaching an industrially relevant environment and a battery-anode pilot announcement with planned scale-up, indicating more than research interest; it does not establish verified commercial sales to established buyers.

processing_requirements.statement: Kraft lignin needs activation or depolymerization before PF resin use; neither chemical-modification equipment nor a lignin dryer is available at the mill, so dry-powder buyers would need to provide drying.
Feedstock compatibility could not be scored because the evidence library has no numeric pathway requirements to compare with the feedstock.

The economics scenarios calculated dry mass and usable dry feedstock, but did not calculate product output, revenue, variable cost, gross contribution, or contribution per tonne because required inputs are missing.

technical_maturity.statement: Evidence gives TRL 8 for biobased phenolic-resin production and TRL 9 for LignoBoost extraction combined with phenol substitution in resins; the latter is the more specifically matched process description.

adoption_barriers.statement: The cited resin route requires activation or depolymerization, while the mill lacks chemical-modification equipment.
Plywood and other wood-panel producers are implied customers, but the evidence does not identify a buyer for this mill or establish that its wet cake meets customer specifications.
Qualification evidence includes EN 314-2 Bonding Class 3 and EN 717-2 emissions testing; the cited laboratory study names its Chinese adhesive standard inconsistently.
Diverting lignin for sale would change its recorded use as internal boiler fuel, and uncertain moisture affects dry tonnage and shipping plans.

commercialization_feasibility.rationale: A resin application and implied wood-panel customer segment are established, but commercialization requires activation or depolymerization, drying arrangements, and buyer qualification; these are significant process and partnership needs rather than existing mill capabilities.

feedstock_compatibility.rationale: The evidence library has no numeric requirements for this pathway to check against.

technical_readiness.rationale: TRL 8 maps to 5. Stated in EV-PF-01#3.

The deterministic feedstock check scores compatibility 1 for carbon-fiber precursor requirements: the supplied lignin content is 88% versus a minimum of 99%, and ash is 3.5% versus a maximum of 0.1%; these checks apply to carbon fiber, not every carbon product.
For activated carbon, the evidence reports no strict precursor-quality limits and says lower ash improves yield; it provides no equivalent formal precursor specification for hard carbon.

documented_facts.statement: For kraft lignin in phenol-formaldehyde (PF) resins, the typical replacement of phenol is up to 50%, using a two-step process with depolymerized lignin (Mw 800-1,700 g/mol).
UPM states that LPF resin is industrially proven and meets EN 314-2 Bonding Class 3 for veneer plywood.
UPM reports formaldehyde emissions (EN 717-2) of 0.230 mg/m²/h for 12 mm spruce, 0.148 for 12 mm birch, and 0.170 for 12 mm combi panels made with LPF resin.
Global PF resin production was expected to reach about 10 Mt (valued at about USD 13.36 billion in 2019), and more than 50% of these resins are used to make adhesives for wood-based panels.
UPM states that its lignin can replace up to 80% of the phenol in lignin-phenol-formaldehyde (LPF) resin.
Kraft lignin needs an activation or depolymerization step before use in PF resins.
Pre-treatment of kraft lignin: Activation or depolymerization is needed before kraft lignin is used in PF resins.
With the depolymerized lignin making up 50% of the phenolic component, the resin's viscosity, bonding strength, and free formaldehyde met the Chinese wood-adhesive standard used in the study.
Replacing 30 wt% of the petroleum-based polyol with unmodified lignin, 16 of the 19 lignins tested gave rigid PUR/PIR foams that passed all measured ASTM C1029-15 type 1 specifications.
Rigid foams containing 19-23% (w/w) hardwood kraft lignin, or 25-30% (w/w) organosolv lignin, kept comparable structure and strength.
Fifteen unmodified lignins (ten kraft, five organosolv) were tested as a replacement for 20 wt% of the petroleum-based polyol in flexible polyurethane foam.
Organosolv lignins were the most suitable for automotive flexible foam; kraft lignins gave denser, stiffer foams that the authors suggest may suit heavy-duty foams.
Two of the three foams that failed were made with kraft lignin; they failed the compressive strength and/or closed-cell content requirements.
Modification of kraft lignin: Kraft lignin needs significant treatment (for example oxypropylation, depolymerization, or liquefaction) to reach target properties for polyurethanes.
Unmodified lignin reduced foam resiliency: compression set rose to 7-32% against 6% for the control, though it stayed within the standard's limit of below 60%.
Commercialization of lignin-based polyurethane foams remains limited by low product consistency, poor technical performance, and high production costs.
The IEA rates polyurethane uses of lignin (foams, panels, coatings, rubber replacement; kraft, organosolv, and soda lignin) at TRL 6.

Oak Ridge National Laboratory (ORNL) specifications for lignin as a carbon fiber precursor (Baker et al. 2005) set lignin content at 99%, ash below 0.1%, volatiles below 5% at 250 °C, and full removal of particulates larger than 1 µm.
None of the lignin samples in the study met the ORNL volatiles specification.
Mechanical properties of lignin-based carbon fibers were about 50% of the target in this work.
Hard carbons from kraft lignin (carbonized at 1,200 °C) had higher initial coulombic efficiency than those from sulfonated lignin, which the review attributes to lower ash content.
Stora Enso announced a EUR 10 million pilot production line for lignin-based anode material, operational in 2021, with scale-up planned in standardized 20 kton manufacturing units.
Activated carbon has no strict limitations on precursor quality, so lignin too impure for other uses can be converted into it.

The modelled production cost of GreenLight lignin-based carbon fiber was EUR 12.6/kg, against about EUR 16/kg estimated for PAN-based fiber; cooperation with existing melt-spinning and carbon fiber plants could lower it to EUR 6.5-7.1/kg.
Stora Enso states that qualification with battery manufacturers and carmakers can take 3 years, and that partnering helps shorten this.
A feedstock comparison for sodium-ion battery hard carbon lists lignin at about 300 $/t with a carbon yield above 40%, against anthracite (50-200 $/t, about 90%) and cellulose (1,000 $/t, below 10%).
Lignin content: Greater than 99% (ORNL precursor specification).
Ash content: Below 0.1% by weight (ORNL precursor specification).
Residual carbohydrates: Below 500 ppm (Baker 2011). Not mapped to the feedstock's carbohydrate percentage, because the source doesn't state the basis of the ppm figure.
Volatile material: Below 5% at 250 °C. The feedstock profile has no volatiles field, so this is not checked.
Particulate matter: 100% removal of particulates larger than 1 µm in diameter.
Purification of kraft lignin: The kraft lignin examined needed purification before it could be used for carbon fiber.
Melt spinnability of softwood lignin: A plasticizing (alloying) agent is needed to melt-spin softwood lignin.
Precursor quality: No strict limitations on precursor quality; lower ash improves yield.
The GreenLight project raised the TRL of lignin precursor fiber production from 2-3 (proof of concept) to 5 (validated in an industrially relevant environment).
A 2018 report cited by the IEA estimates the technology readiness level (TRL) for producing biobased phenolic resins at 8.
A techno-economic comparison lists LignoBoost extraction combined with phenol substitution in resins ('LB+Resin') at TRL 9.

Total hydroxyl value of the lignin: Above 200 mg KOH/g (3.56 mmol/g total OH) is cited as the acceptable range for rigid polyurethane foam production. This is total OH, not phenolic OH, so it is not checked against the feedstock's phenolic OH figure.
